articles.summary:
What are the relationships and dominant interests in play, as the summit kicks off after a bitter row over its hosting?

Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.

articles.title: Saudi Aramco tower damaged after Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh
articles.summary:
Saudi Aramco tower damaged after Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh

Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 11/08/2026 - 09:35
The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted ballistic and cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions
Flames burn at an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, 3 October 2026 (AFP)
Off

A building belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco was damaged in Riyadh on Sunday as Saudi Arabia reported a series of missile attacks launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement.

An official at Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said Aramco's administrative building sustained minor damage after falling shrapnel struck it. 

No injuries or deaths were reported, the official said, adding that the relevant authorities had responded and taken the necessary measures.

A Reuters witness reported seeing windows blown out across several floors of the Aramco Tower in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD), one of the Saudi capital’s main business districts.

The damage followed reports of loud explosions in Riyadh and an early-warning alert issued by Saudi Civil Defence. Authorities later said the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched towards Riyadh on Sunday. 

It later reported intercepting two cruise missiles in the capital and the kingdom’s southern region.

Earlier, coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki said another ballistic missile launched towards the Eastern Province had been intercepted.

The developments came amid escalating fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, following the collapse of a 2022 truce and renewed military operations in Yemen. 

Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
Read More »

The latest missile interceptions came a day after the Houthi-run Health Ministry said Saudi-led coalition air strikes had killed at least 33 people, including eight women and 13 children, in the village of al-Shariyah near Sanaa.

Health Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said at least 39 others were wounded in Saturday’s attacks, which he said targeted homes, roads, paramedics and Civil Defence teams in the Bani Hushaish district, east of the capital.

There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on the reported strikes, and Al Jazeera said it could not independently verify the casualty figures.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree also claimed that the coalition had carried out 105 air strikes and missile attacks over 24 hours, targeting Sanaa and seven other governorates. 

He put the total number of attacks since the latest escalation began at 4,369.

Saree said the Houthis had carried out six operations targeting Aramco facilities, Riyadh airport and Saudi military positions on both sides of the border.  

The latest escalation follows a campaign launched by Yemen’s internationally recognised government last month to retake territory held by the Houthis, including Sanaa. The group has controlled the capital since 2014.

articles.title: IRGC dismisses new US plan to tighten economic pressure on Iran as 'wordplay'
articles.summary:
IRGC dismisses new US plan to tighten economic pressure on Iran as 'wordplay'

The US cannot achieve its goals of blockading Iran's economy and shutting its trade routes because Tehran has made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours, a Revolutionary Guards spokesperson was quoted as saying on Sunday.

Hossein Mohebbi was reacting to the US military's Task Force Iron Gate, launched to help crack down on Tehran's movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the Caspian Sea.

"The Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, the Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach," Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency.

Reporting by Reuters

articles.title: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged by falling debris in attempted attack, ministry says
articles.summary:
Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged by falling debris in attempted attack, ministry says

An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom's Energy Ministry said.

A witness told Reuters that they saw blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital's King Abdullah Financial District.

The incident, which the ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis towards Riyadh.

Aramco was not immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the Houthis.

Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led coalition subsequently said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the kingdom's southern region.

Reporting by Reuters

Naturalists divided over potential impact of proposals to increase number of wild raptors in England and Wales

White-tailed eagles reintroduced into England and Wales imperil endangered seabird populations and risk wiping out some colonies, ecologists and conservationists are warning.

Puffins, guillemots, razorbills, fulmars and kittiwakes are among the birds for which breeding populations could collapse if large numbers of white-tailed eagles are released, according to some academics and conservationists.
